title: Ashtpadi 15, salok: all powers
hookLine: sarab kalaa bharpoor: He is full of every power (Sukhmani 15)

lines: AFTER GOOD NEWS, AND AFTER BAD.
WHERE DOES THE RISING COME FROM?
cards: Ask a Sikh how they're doing and you might hear two words: chardi kalaa. It can be said after good news, and after bad. A flooded basement, a hard diagnosis, a lost job, and still: chardi kalaa.
Rising spirits. Ever-ascending energy. It's a deeply Sikh phrase, and it can sound almost stubborn, cheerful in the face of everything.
But where does that rising energy come from? The answer is hiding in the second word, kalaa, and today the salok of the fifteenth ashtpadi puts that word at its center.

teach.b: The salok, in paraphrase: God is brimful of every power, the knower of every pain. By remembering Him we are carried across; Nanak is a sacrifice to Him. Three words.
Sarab: all, every. Bharpoor: brimful, full to the edge, like a bucket that can't take one more drop. And kalaa, a rich word.

teach.h: KALAA: POWER, ART, A SLIVER OF MOON.
teach.b: It can mean power, but also skill, art, a craft, and in older Indian usage, a phase of the moon, one sliver of its light.
So sarab kalaa bharpoor is something like: full to the brim with every power, every art, every light there is. In the salok's picture, there is no power anywhere that isn't already full in the One.

Now come back to chardi kalaa. Read beside this salok, rising power isn't a boast of home-made strength. It points the other way: the power rising in a person comes from the One who is full of all of it.

Spirits can rise after a flood because, in this picture, the source isn't the basement. That's why the salok's second half matters. The One full of every power is also birthaa jaananhaar, the knower of every pain.
All that power isn't cold or far away; it knows what's hurting. We stay with that half tomorrow.
Today, one picture: beside sarab kalaa bharpoor, every person is small. The salok doesn't make that frightening.
Being small beside the One full of every power, who also knows every pain, is pictured as being held.

how: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib open the fifteenth ashtpadi with the salok sarab kalaa bharpoor, and in daily life chardi kalaa, rising spirits, is an answer Sikhs give to 'how are you?', in good times and hard ones.

o: a fixed rule that cannot be bent
a dark mood that comes and goes
power, skill, art, a sliver of light

games.q: the salok of ashtpadi 15 — tap the pairs.
p: power, art, a sliver of moon

s: chardi kalaa is a boast that Sikhs are strong on their own
read beside the salok, the rising power comes from the One who is sarab kalaa bharpoor.
kalaa can mean power, skill or art, and a phase of the moon
a rich word: every power, every art, every light.
the salok pictures God's power as cold and far away
the same line calls the One the knower of every pain.

games.q: your basement just flooded. a Sikh neighbor asks how you are and then answers her own question: chardi kalaa. what does she mean?
o: that spirits can rise because their source isn't the basement.
games.why: chardi kalaa is rising power, drawn from the One who is full of every power, not a denial of the flood.

practice: If you can see the sky, look at it; if not, picture the night sky, star past star, and let yourself be the size you actually are, noticing any fear in that.
Then hold the salok's picture instead: everything out there brimful of one power, and that power knowing you, small and held. Let your breathing slow into it, and if you pray, say Waheguru softly.

wordCard.voice: Kalaa, power, skill, art. Sarab kalaa bharpoor, brimful of every power, and the knower of every pain. The same kalaa rises in chardi kalaa.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kalaa, power, skill or art; the same word as in chardi kalaa.

carryVoice: Your line: he holds all power. Small, and held by the One who knows every pain. Day four hundred ninety-four counts.
